https://ryangoldbacher.com/about/"

About Ryan Goldbacher

Tour Manager · Production Manager · FOH Audio Engineer 

  <p>Ryan Goldbacher is a touring audio engineer, tour manager, and production manager. He's spent more than twenty years on the road, mixing front of house and running tours for artists across rock, punk, country, and heavy metal.</p>

  <section style="margin-bottom: 3rem;">
    <h2>First live sound</h2>
    <p>He didn't set out to do this. He was a guitarist who went to <strong>Charter Tech</strong>, a performing arts high school in New Jersey, because the academics were better than the local public option. He had to declare a major, and guitar was the only thing he had any real interest in, so that's what he picked. Then the school brought in music technology, and a teacher named <strong>Lew London</strong> — a jazz guitarist who played in the <strong>Bubba Mac Blues Band</strong> — noticed Ryan sitting in the music room every day, noodling on guitar while he waited for a ride home.</p>

    <p><strong>Lew</strong> called him over to a computer running an early version of Pro Tools and asked if he wanted to learn it.</p>

    <p><em>"That's a dumb name for a piece of software. What the heck is Pro Tools?"</em></p>

    <p>Then Ryan sat down with it and found something out. He couldn't play the way he wanted to. But he could listen. And he could use the DAW like a word processor — cut, delete, move things around, hear what changed. That was the click. It's the thing he's been chasing ever since.</p>
  </section>

  <section style="margin-bottom: 3rem;">
    <h2>The road</h2>
    <p>The touring career came together fast. <strong>Bill Anderson</strong> was early — a country legend who'd written more hits than almost anyone, and who told stories about <strong>Dolly Parton</strong> and <strong>George Strait</strong> and <strong>Little Jimmy Dickens</strong> like they were just people he knew. No pretense, no ego. Just another day at work, with legends in the room. Ryan learned from the way Bill talked about all of it — nothing was a big deal, and that was the whole point.</p>

    <p>Then <strong>Shooter Jennings</strong>. That one came sideways. Ryan was working at <strong>SIR</strong> as a rehearsal tech when <strong>Evanescence</strong>'s manager called him by mistake, thinking he was another engineer. Ryan corrected him, then said the thing that changed his career: I'm still interested in the gig. <strong>Andy</strong> called back a few days later and asked if Ryan had ever tour-managed. He hadn't. He said yes anyway.</p>

    <p>That first tour was the education of a lifetime, mostly because of everything he didn't know. He had no idea how to settle a show. He had no real understanding that not every promoter plays straight. He made mistakes early — the kind that cost real money — and had to learn the hard way that this job is equal parts logistics, people skills, and knowing when to push back.</p>

    <p>Everything after came from that first yes. <strong>Gavin DeGraw</strong>, <strong>Bayside</strong>, <strong>The Record Company</strong>, <strong>Stiff Little Fingers</strong>, <strong>Black Star Riders and Thin Lizzy</strong>, <strong>Samantha Fish</strong>, <strong>Accept</strong>, <strong>Mr. Big</strong>, <strong>The HU</strong>, <strong>Pop Evil</strong>, and now <strong>Tom Keifer</strong>. Country, punk, hard rock, folk-metal, legacy acts. He worked as tour manager, production manager, FOH engineer, and monitor engineer — sometimes all of them on the same run. The genre never mattered as much as whether the show happened and sounded right.</p>
  </section>

  <section style="margin-bottom: 3rem;">
    <h2>What he actually believes about mixing</h2>
    <p>Ryan has a specific view of what the job is. It's not to impress other engineers. It's not to show off gear. It's not to chase a spec sheet.</p>

    <p><em>"There's two people I'm trying to impress every night — myself and the guy signing my check in the middle of the stage."</em></p>

    <p>A good mix is tight. It's cohesive. It sounds like a band playing in a room, not like a pile of tracks fighting each other. When he hears a front-of-house mix that puts everything on the kick drum and nothing on the rest of the band, he calls it out plainly — that's not a mix, that's a drum solo with accompaniment.</p>

    <p>His technical philosophy follows from the same place. <em>"Never think of the kick drum as a bass drum. It's a very full range instrument."</em> He doesn't load the sub with kick. He lets the bass do the low-end lifting, on purpose, and keeps the kick punchy in the range where it actually reads. It's a small distinction that changes how a whole band sits together.</p>

    <p>And when someone asks him for a rule: <em>"There's no rules for any of this. My opinion shouldn't matter that much unless it's going to get you fired. Turn the knobs till it sounds good to you."</em></p>
  </section>

  <section style="margin-bottom: 3rem;">
    <h2>Leadership</h2>
    <p>Early in his management career, Ryan had what he now calls a <em>"very immature idea of what a leader should be."</em> <em>"I was the boss. I was, 'Do this. You don't get to have a say.'"</em></p>

    <p>The road corrected him. On a bus, across time zones, under pressure, you can't just give orders — you have to build trust. Letting people solve problems their own way, and trusting them to be good at their jobs, works better than any structure he could impose. That's the advice he gives young tour managers now. Not the logistics — the leadership.</p>
  </section>

  <section style="margin-bottom: 3rem;">
    <h2>The work now</h2>
    <p>Ryan currently mixes FOH for <strong>Tom Keifer</strong> and runs tour and production management for a rotating roster of artists. He's also the voice behind <strong>@RyanTheGoldbacher</strong>, where he makes short-form videos about the craft and about the industry itself — kick drum technique, why a mix has to be tight before it can be loud, why the sound of a console matters more than its spec sheet, what it actually takes to survive a career on the road. He's a vocal advocate for the working engineer: proper pay, proper hospitality, and proper respect for the crew that makes the show happen.</p>

    <p>He still believes the best way to learn this job is to be in the room with people who know more than you do, and the clearest signal of a professional is how they treat the people around them.</p>
  </section>
</div>

items.title: Digico Console Opinion
items.content:
https://ryangoldbacher.com/blog/2026-09-20-digico-console-opinion/"

Console Philosophy & Gear Opinions

Why I Don't Use DiGiCo Consoles — And What I Use Instead

By Ryan Goldbacher · September 20, 2026

    <div style="color: var(--muted); line-height: 1.7;">
      <h2>What console does Ryan Goldbacher use?</h2>


      <p><strong>Short answer:</strong> I'm not a DiGiCo fan. I've mixed on them, I know engineers who get great results on them, and they're reliable — they're just not my tool. I currently mix on Allen & Heath, and from what I've heard, the Yamaha DM7 and PM series are probably the best-sounding digital desks out there right now.</p>

      <p>This isn't a brand war. It's about what lets me work the way I need to work.</p>

      <h2>My Console History in One Paragraph</h2>

      <p>I started on analog — PM5D was just coming out when I began touring, M7CL was the cheaper version. They were reliable, you could get a mix going, but they lacked sonically. The first digital consoles that actually sounded good were the Pro Series and Avid Venue (first ones you could run plugins on). I knew Pro Tools from studio work, so Avid made sense. But nowadays I'm Allen & Heath. I like the way they sound, I'm good at getting them sounding good, and that's what matters.</p>

      <h2>Why Not DiGiCo?</h2>

      <p>I made a video about this that went viral on Instagram and Facebook — not because I was trying to start something, but because I said what I actually think. The core of it:</p>

      <ul>
        <li><strong>Sound character:</strong> "A $150k price tag doesn't buy you a good sounding desk." To my ears, DiGiCo sounds clinical — what I call "hospital hallway" sound. Clean, sterile, no grit.</li>
        <li><strong>What I want:</strong> "I want a console that fights me back a little bit and have it punch me in the gut than have it be super clean." I want character, tension, something that pushes back.</li>
        <li><strong>Fader feel:</strong> Multiple engineers have commented the fader quality feels cheap. That matters when you're riding faders for two hours a night.</li>
      </ul>

      <p>When DiGiCo's official Instagram account replied to my roast with "Much respect to you!" — I replied "I still have respect for all the DiGiBros." That's the point. People get great mixes on DiGiCo. It's just not my pair of shoes.</p>

      <h2>What I Use Instead: Allen & Heath</h2>

      <p>Right now I'm an Allen & Heath guy. Here's why:</p>

      <ul>
        <li><strong>Sound:</strong> I like the way they sound. The preamps have the "grit" I'm looking for — what one commenter called "the preamps might be 'clean', but the tension is filthy."</li>
        <li><strong>Workflow:</strong> I'm good at getting them sounding good. That's not marketing — that's 20+ years of turning knobs until it works.</li>
        <li><strong>Value:</strong> I have an Allen & Heath SQ rack mount that has more inputs than my PM5D did 20 years ago, and the PM5D was almost $100k when it came out.</li>
      </ul>

      <h2>What I'd Use If I Wasn't on Allen & Heath: Yamaha</h2>

      <p>I don't have a ton of seat time on the new Yamaha DM7 and PM series, but what I have used tells me: <strong>they're probably the best sounding desks out there.</strong> Yamaha's been refining digital console sound for decades — PM5D, M7CL, PM10, Rivage — each generation gets closer. If you want clinical precision that still has musicality, that's the direction.</p>

      <h2>The Philosophy: "It's Just a Pair of Shoes"</h2>

      <p>This is the hill I'll die on: <strong>Your console is a tool. Use the one that fits you.</strong></p>

      <blockquote>
        "It's just a pair of shoes that you're comfortable with, you know? If you can figure out how to make it work for you, it doesn't matter what anybody else thinks."
      </blockquote>

      <p>I've seen engineers refuse gigs because the house console wasn't their preferred brand. That's the wrong mindset. If you're so married to a piece of gear that you can't work without it, you're not an engineer — you're a template runner.</p>

      <p>People get killer mixes on X32s. People get killer mixes on DiGiCo. People get killer mixes on analog Heritage 3000s. The console doesn't make the mix. <strong>You do.</strong></p>

      <h2>Digital Console Evolution: What Actually Changed</h2>

      <p>For context — I've lived through the entire digital console transition:</p>

      <table style="width: 100%; border-collapse: collapse; margin: 1.5rem 0;">
        <thead>
          <tr>
            <th scope="col" style="border: 1px solid #ddd; padding: 8px; background: #f4f4f4;">Era</th>
            <th scope="col" style="border: 1px solid #ddd; padding: 8px; background: #f4f4f4;">Consoles</th>
            <th scope="col" style="border: 1px solid #ddd; padding: 8px; background: #f4f4f4;">Reality</th>
          </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr>
            <td style="border: 1px solid #ddd; padding: 8px;">Early 2000s</td>
            <td style="border: 1px solid #ddd; padding: 8px;">PM5D, M7CL</td>
            <td style="border: 1px solid #ddd; padding: 8px;">Reliable, workflow OK, sonically lacking</td>
          </tr>
          <tr>
            <td style="border: 1px solid #ddd; padding: 8px;">Mid 2000s</td>
            <td style="border: 1px solid #ddd; padding: 8px;">Avid Venue, Pro Series</td>
            <td style="border: 1px solid #ddd; padding: 8px;">First good-sounding digital, plugin integration</td>
          </tr>
          <tr>
            <td style="border: 1px solid #ddd; padding: 8px;">2010s</td>
            <td style="border: 1px solid #ddd; padding: 8px;">DiGiCo SD series, Yamaha Rivage, Midas Pro</td>
            <td style="border: 1px solid #ddd; padding: 8px;">Everything got usable; brand preference dominates</td>
          </tr>
          <tr>
            <td style="border: 1px solid #ddd; padding: 8px;">2020s</td>
            <td style="border: 1px solid #ddd; padding: 8px;">DM7, Quantum, Avantis, SQ</td>
            <td style="border: 1px solid #ddd; padding: 8px;">Rack mounts out-spec 2000s flagships at 1/10 the price</td>
          </tr>
        </tbody>
      </table>

      <p>The gap between "pro" and "entry level" has collapsed. An SQ has more I/O than a PM5D. The engineering is there at every price point now. The difference is workflow, sound character, and ecosystem — not capability.</p>

      <h2>What This Means for You</h2>

      <p>If you're choosing a console — for a tour, an install, a venue — here's my framework:</p>

      <ol>
        <li><strong>Can you get a mix on it?</strong> Yes? Good. Move on.</li>
        <li><strong>Does the workflow match how you think?</strong> Some consoles fight you; some get out of your way.</li>
        <li><strong>Does the sound character serve the music?</strong> Clean isn't always better. Grit isn't always better. Match the tool to the gig.</li>
        <li><strong>Can you fix it when it breaks?</strong> Reliability, parts availability, local support — boring but critical.</li>
        <li><strong>Stop reading reviews. Start turning knobs.</strong> You'll learn 10x more in one soundcheck than a year of forum debates.</li>
      </ol>

      <h2>Frequently Asked Questions</h2>

      <p><strong>Is DiGiCo a bad console?</strong><br>No. It's reliable, widely used, and plenty of top engineers choose it. It's just not my preference.</p>

      <p><strong>What's the best live sound console?</strong><br>There isn't one. The best console is the one you know deeply enough to push to its limits. For me that's Allen & Heath. For you it might be DiGiCo, Yamaha, Midas, or Avid.</p>

      <p><strong>Do you hate digital consoles?</strong><br>No. I started in studios on Pro Tools. I've mixed on every major digital platform. I just prefer consoles with character over clinical precision.</p>

      <p><strong>What console would you recommend for a small venue?</strong><br>Whatever fits the budget and the operator. Allen & Heath SQ, Yamaha TF/CL, Midas M32, Behringer X32 — they'll all do the job if you know how to use them.</p>

    </div>
  </article>
</div>

items.title: Technical Philosophy Learn By Doing
items.content:
https://ryangoldbacher.com/blog/2026-09-20-technical-philosophy-learn-by-doing/"

Technical Philosophy

Why I Believe in Learning by Doing — Not Degrees

By Ryan Goldbacher · September 20, 2026

    <div style="color: var(--muted); line-height: 1.7;">
      <p><strong>A goal with a degree is overrated if you really do want to be an audio engineer</strong> — just because it's so expensive.</p>

      <p>That's what I've said in multiple interviews and YouTube videos. And I mean it. I've actually worked for a couple sound companies that did exactly what I wish more would do: they set aside time to just play around. The young guys were totally encouraged to pop the lid on a console and play around on the equipment — hands-on doing it in an environment where you're not going to get fired for doing it wrong.</p>

      <p>That builds a comfort zone for me — and for anyone learning. When I started, this was intimidating — not because I didn't know what everything did, but because I didn't know what would happen if I turned that knob.</p>

      <p>Being able to do that in a controlled environment gives you a lot of confidence. Especially when no one's looking over your shoulder and you're going at the speed of your comfort — as opposed to oh, I've got 45 minutes to cover this, you got a band breathing down your neck.</p>

      <h2>The "Safe Failure" Principle</h2>

      <p>I think sound companies should set aside time to just play around where you're not going to get fired for doing it wrong. This is crucial for building real skill.</p>

      <p>One of my earliest lessons: "You'll learn 10 times more from doing stuff than by studying stuff." This isn't just a saying — it's a truth I've lived through decades of touring. Reading about how to mix a kick drum in a stadium won't prepare you for when the guitar player is playing too loud and the singer can't hear themselves in a 10,000-seat venue.</p>

      <h2>Know Your Limits — But Test Them</h2>

      <p>Another key principle I live by: "Test your limits, but don't be afraid to know where they are."</p>

      <p>This means pushing yourself to grow, but also being honest about where you need more experience. In live sound, ego can get people hurt — or at least get the mix hurt. Knowing when to ask for help or when you need more practice on a specific skill is just as important as being confident in what you do know.</p>

      <p>I've seen engineers try to fake their way through things they don't understand, and it never ends well. Better to say "I'm not 100% sure on this — can we test it during soundcheck?" than to pretend you know and ruin the show.</p>

      <h2>My Hands-On Learning Journey</h2>

      <p>My own journey proves this philosophy. I didn't start with a degree — I started by realizing I couldn't play guitar but could listen. Then I got hands-on with Pro Tools in high school, which led to an internship at Darkhorse Studios, then work at SIR as a rehearsal and backline technician, and eventually my break with Evanescence that led to touring with Shooter Jennings.</p>

      <p>Each step was about doing, not just studying:</p>

      <ul>
        <li><strong>High School:</strong> Learning Pro Tools by actually using it</li>
        <li><strong>Darkhorse Internship:</strong> Watching and assisting experienced engineers</li>
        <li><strong>SIR Work:</strong> Hands-on with rehearsal setups and backline gear</li>
        <li><strong>Evanescence Connection:</strong> Stepping up when opportunity knocked</li>
        <li><strong>Shooter Jennings:</strong> My first tour management role — "fake it till you make it" in the best sense</li>
      </ul>

      <h2>The Real World vs. Classroom</h2>

      <p>Let me be clear — I'm not against education. But in live sound engineering specifically, the skills that matter most are learned on the job:</p>

      <ul>
        <li><strong>Reading the room:</strong> How to adjust your mix based on venue acoustics, crowd energy, and band dynamics</li>
        <li><strong>Artist communication:</strong> Learning what each musician needs to hear in their monitors</li>
        <li><strong>Problem-solving under pressure:</strong> When something goes wrong 10 minutes before showtime</li>
        <li><strong>Gear familiarity:</strong> Knowing how different consoles, speakers, and instruments actually sound in practice</li>
        <li><strong>Tour logistics:</strong> How to move people and equipment efficiently across cities and countries</li>
      </ul>

      <p>These aren't things you learn from a textbook. These are things you learn by doing, making mistakes, and getting better each time.</p>

      <h2>Advice for Aspiring Engineers</h2>

      <p>If you're trying to break into live sound engineering, here's my practical advice:</p>

      <ol>
        <li><strong>Start where you can:</strong> Look for internships, volunteer opportunities, or entry-level positions at local venues, churches, or rental companies.</li>
        <li><strong>Ask to touch the gear:</strong> Don't just watch — ask if you can help patch, set up mics, or run cables during soundcheck.</li>
        <li><strong>Embrace the "safe failure" mindset:</strong> Find environments where you can experiment without catastrophic consequences.</li>
        <li><strong>Learn one thing deeply:</strong> Instead of trying to know everything about everything, become really good at one area (like vocal mixing or drum tuning) and build from there.</li>
        <li><strong>Document your journey:</strong> Keep notes on what you learn each day — what worked, what didn't, and why.</li>
        <li><strong>Network authentically:</strong> Build real relationships with people in the industry — not just collecting contacts, but actually learning from others.</li>
      </ol>

      <h2>The Bottom Line</h2>

      <p>In my 20+ years of touring with artists like Tom Keifer, Sebastian Bach, Accept, and The HU, I've never once been asked for my diploma or degree certificate. I've been asked:</p>

      <ul>
        <li>Can you mix this band's show?</li>
        <li>Can you handle the tour logistics?</li>
        <li>Can you communicate effectively with the artist and crew?</li>
        <li>Can you solve problems quickly when they arise?</li>
      </ul>

      <p>Those are skills you only learn by doing. So if you're passionate about live sound, get your hands on some equipment — even if it's just a basic mixer or some used gear. Start small, make mistakes, learn from them, and keep going.</p>

      <p>Remember: You'll learn 10 times more from doing stuff than by studying stuff. And that's exactly how you build a real career in this industry.</p>
